content.title: About
content.content: Frozen berries are a blend of berries (strawberry, raspberry, blueberry, blackberry, etc.) harvested at peak ripeness and quickly frozen to preserve flavor, aroma, and nutrients. They are convenient for cooking and allow you to enjoy berry taste year‑round.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Berries are flash‑frozen within minutes of picking to lock in freshness.
The mix often includes several varieties, providing a diverse taste and color profile.
Freezing retains most of the vitamin C, vitamin K, and antioxidant content.
Frozen berries are popular in smoothies, baked goods, sauces, and desserts.
Freezing reduces nutrient loss compared with prolonged storage of fresh berries.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Berries contain anthocyanins and vitamin C, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Flavonoids improve vessel function and may lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Fiber in berries promotes healthy gut motility and satiety.

items.title: Low‑calorie snack
items.content: Berries are low in calories, making them a good choice for weight management.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Berries provide vitamin K, manganese, potassium, and folate, important for bone health and metabolism.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to specific berries.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Berries are naturally sweet; people with diabetes should consider their glycemic impact.

items.title: Ice crystal formation
items.content: Improper storage can lead to large ice crystals, affecting texture.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add frozen berries to smoothies, yogurt, oatmeal, baked goods, sauces, or ice cream. They can be thawed in the refrigerator or used directly from the freezer.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight bag or container at –18 °C. Once thawed, consume within 1–2 days and do not refreeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Candy sprinkles are tiny sweet pieces made from sugar, starch and food‑grade colorants. They are used to decorate desserts, baked goods, ice cream and drinks, adding a bright look and a light sweet note.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sprinkles first appeared in the United States in the early 1920s and quickly became a staple in confectionery.
More than 100 colors and shapes exist, from classic round “non‑pareils” to stars and hearts.
Most sprinkles are gluten‑free, but may contain trace amounts of nuts or soy.
Sugar sprinkles are a common topping for celebration cakes, especially at children’s parties.
In some countries, such as Japan, “wet” sprinkles coated with a glossy glaze are popular.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Sprinkles contain simple sugars that provide rapid energy, useful in small amounts for children or athletes.

items.title: Visual stimulation
items.content: Bright colors can enhance appetite and improve mood, particularly for kids.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption may contribute to weight gain, tooth decay and blood‑glucose spikes.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Some sprinkles contain food colorings derived from allergenic sources such as soy.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Certain varieties use artificial dyes and preservatives that can cause sensitivity in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add sprinkles at the end of preparation: sprinkle over cupcakes, cakes, cookies, ice cream, yogurt, smoothies and even coffee. Lightly dust with powdered sugar for a more even distribution if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sprinkles in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from moisture and direct sunlight. Properly stored, they retain color and crunch for up to 12 months.

cornish-game-hen-cooked-skin-eaten.title: Cornish game hen, cooked, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: The Cornish game hen is a small domestic bird weighing about 500–700 g, often served whole. When cooked with the skin on, it stays juicy and flavorful, while the skin becomes crisp. The bird is rich in protein, B‑vitamins, and minerals, making it a popular choice for quick, nutritious meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The Cornish game hen originates from a cross between the British Cornish breed and the American White Rock.
Its small size makes it a “baby” chicken, but the meat tastes comparable to that of a regular chicken.
Chefs love it because a whole bird can be roasted in a short time, perfect for plating.
During roasting the skin forms a natural barrier that locks in juices.
In the United States it is frequently served in restaurants as a single‑portion chicken.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of cooked meat provides about 25 g of high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat contains niacin (B3), vitamin B6, and folate, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Cornish game hen supplies iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for blood health and bones.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Makes it suitable for low‑carb and keto diets.

items.title: Healthy fats in the skin
items.content: The skin contains monounsaturated fats that can support heart health when eaten in moderation.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to bird meat.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the skin is seasoned heavily with salt, it can become a significant source of sodium.

items.title: Potential bacteria
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor salmonella; ensure the internal temperature reaches 74 °C.

items.title: Cholesterol
items.content: The skin contains more cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should limit consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cornish game hen can be roasted, grilled, or pan‑seared. After cooking, the crisp skin can be eaten as a tasty garnish, and the meat sliced into portions. It pairs well with herbs, lemon, garlic, and light sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw meat in the refrigerator at +2–4 °C for up to 2 days. Cooked hen should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days or frozen for up to 2 months. Reheat cooked meat to an internal temperature of 74 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑fat evaporated milk (2 %) is a dairy product made by removing most of the water from regular milk and adding a modest amount of sugar. It retains most of milk’s nutrients while offering lower calories and fat compared with traditional sweetened condensed milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Evaporated milk was invented in the 19th century as a way to preserve milk without refrigeration.
The reduced‑fat version appeared later as consumers sought lighter alternatives.
Typical sugar content in sweetened versions is about 55 % of the product’s weight.
Its thick texture makes it popular in desserts, confectionery, and beverages.
In many countries evaporated milk is a traditional ingredient for holiday cakes and puddings.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Evaporated milk provides a high amount of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Despite the low fat, it still supplies about 7 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains riboflavin (B2) and vitamin B12, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: With only 2 % fat, it fits better into calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Adds creaminess without extra fat
items.content: Its dense consistency allows it to give a creamy mouthfeel to dishes without needing additional butter or oil.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The added sugar can raise blood glucose levels and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The product contains lactose, so those who are intolerant should choose lactose‑free alternatives.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may experience reactions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Even with reduced fat, the sugar makes it relatively calorie‑dense.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reduced‑fat evaporated milk is used in baking, custards, ice cream, sweet sauces, and beverages. It can be reconstituted with water or added to coffee for a sweet, low‑fat flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened can in a cool, dry place. After opening, store in the refrigerator and use within 2–3 weeks. Discard if it develops a sour smell or off‑color.

content.title: About
content.content: Roll white hard (2417) is a crunchy bread product made from wheat flour, water, salt and yeast. Baked until a golden crust forms, it has a dense structure and a neutral taste, making it a versatile base for sandwiches, snacks and culinary creations.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The firm crust is created by a long bake at high temperature.
The white colour is achieved by using refined flour without whole‑grain additives.
Traditionally, this type of roll is popular in European cuisine as a mini‑baguette.
Sales of similar rolls in Russia grew by more than 15 % in the 2020s due to rising demand for ready‑to‑eat snacks.
Its thin yet sturdy structure allows slicing into small pieces without crumbling.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: The roll provides a quick source of energy through easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Compared with many baked goods, the hard white roll contains minimal fat.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour used in the recipe supplies thiamine, niacin and folate, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Although not whole‑grain, the roll still offers a modest amount of fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Versatile pairing
items.content: Its neutral flavour allows combination with a wide range of toppings, enhancing nutritional value when paired wisely.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The roll contains wheat flour, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: It can raise blood sugar quickly, which may be undesirable for diabetics.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: For blood‑pressure control, choose low‑salt versions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The hard white roll can be sliced and used in sandwiches, as a base for canapés, in soups as croutons, or served with dips. Lightly toasting it enhances the crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the roll in a dry, cool place in an airtight package. For longer storage keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent drying out.
